text_preview: Chapter 2 Deployment Scenarios

text: This document focuses on cloud deployment scenarios B and C \(including both variants C.1 and C.2\), as defined in the O-RAN Cloud Architecture document \[1\]. The current version of this document focuses on SA NR gNBs deployed on the O-Cloud. The extensions of O-Cloud, if required, to support NSA scenarios indicated in the annexes of the O-RAN Cloud Architecture document \[1\] are FFS.
text_preview: This document focuses on cloud deployment scenarios B and C, including variants C.1 and C.2, as defined in the O-RAN Cloud Architecture document [1]. It primarily covers SA NR gNBs deployed on the O-Cloud. Extensions to support NSA scenarios (as indicated in annexes of [1]) are FFS.

text: O-Clouds are deployed at both regional and edge locations. At a given location, the edge O-Cloud can scale from a single server to a clustered configuration with possibly hundreds of servers. This version of the document focuses on a container- based cloud platform \(see Ch.5.2 for a reference design example\) and it will address VM-based designs in a future release. For the time synchronization aspects, this version of the document focuses on the LLS-C3 configuration \[2\], i.e., O-DU and O-RU are synchronized from the fronthaul network \(see Ch.5.3 for a reference design example\).
text_preview: O-Clouds are deployed at regional and edge locations. The edge cloud can scale from one server to hundreds of servers. This document focuses on container-based cloud platforms, using the LLS-C3 configuration for time synchronization, where O-DU and O-RU are synchronized from the fronthaul network.

text: The terms, vO-CU and vO-DU, represent virtualized or containerized O-CU and O-DU, and are used interchangeably with O-CU and O-DU in this document. The optional use of a Front-haul Gateway \(FHGW\) in the architecture allows significant savings in providing transport between the O-RU and O-DU functionalities.

text: As Figure 2-1 shows, deployment of a cloud platform occurs in two locations: regional and edge clouds. The physical environment of a regional cloud is typically a modern data center, hosting standard server racks with a 19-inch wide rack enclosure, 42U height, and external depth between 1 and 1.2 meters. In this environment, the cloud platform hardware can use standard rack-mount servers and switches, and does not impose special requirements on the hardware form factors.
text_preview: As Figure 2-1 shows, cloud deployment occurs in two locations: regional and edge clouds. Regional clouds are typically housed in modern data centers with standard server racks (19-inch wide, 42U height). This environment accommodates standard rack-mount servers and switches without special hardware requirements.

text: The edge cloud often resides in a traditional telecommunications equipment room with limited space, cooling capacity, floor loading, and so forth. The limitations can impose special requirements on the cloud platform hardware that may require telecommunications standard certifications, such as the Network Equipment Building System \(NEBS\) requirements found in GR-63-CORE \[3\] and GR-1089-CORE \[4\]. For example, the Open Telecom IT Infrastructure \(OTII\) Project specifies a 2U rack server with depth less than 450 mm \[5\]\[3\]. In addition, the Open Compute Project \(OCP\) operates an openEDGE project \[6\], which specifies a compact cloud platform that has the extended environmental requirements often needed in edge deployments.

text: A distinction is made between the O-Cloud network and the fronthaul network. The O-Cloud network includes all switches and routers in any network path between two O-Cloud nodes. The fronthaul network includes all switches and other transport equipment in any network path between an O-DU capable O-Cloud node and an O-RU. These networks may overlap, with some routers/switches \(e.g., the leaf and spine switches in the O-Cloud resource pool\) participating in both the O-Cloud network and the fronthaul network. In the case of such overlap, irrespective of the management responsibilities associated with fabric and transport network elements, all network elements in the timing transfer path between the Grandmaster Clock\(s\) and Slave \(subordinate\) Clocks are considered to be part of the fronthaul synchronization network from the associated synchronization functionality and profile compliance point of view.

text:
* \(1\) All O-DU capable O-Cloud nodes shall have at-least one NIC connected to the fronthaul network. Such nodes shall implement PTP Slaves \(subordinate\) to the fronthaul network that provides the PTP timing synchronization.
  * \(2\) The PTP Slave \(subordinate\) NICs shall support T-TSC functionality that is fully compliant with PTP profile ITU-T G.8275.1.
  * \(3\) These Slave \(subordinate\) PTP NICs shall implement according to "1588-2008 IEEE Standard for a Precision Clock Synchronization Protocol for Networked Measurement and Control Systems", section "6.6.5 Generation of PTP message timestamps" reference point A.
  * \(4\) The O-Cloud shall track which nodes supports PTP capable NICs that are connected to the fronthaul network for the purpose of inventorying O-Cloud nodes that satisfy vO-DU synchronization requirements.
  * \(5\) The O-Cloud shall provide the ability to configure an O-Cloud node's PTP physical port\(s\) that receives PTP traffic as a PTP Slave \(subordinate\). The following minimum configuration shall be supported:
  * Network Transport G.8275.1 synchronization over Ethernet \(Layer 2\);
  * Time Stamping support for hardware time stamping.
  * \(6\) The O-Cloud operating environment \(software stack\) shall support PTP protocol implementation \(1588-2008 IEEE Standard\). For example: in the case when an O-Cloud is based on the Linux OS, this will require support for ptp4l and phc2sys.
  * \(7\) The node clock on each node shall be synchronized from the NIC T-TSC clock\(s\). For example: in the case when an O-Cloud is based on the Linux OS, this will require support for phc2sys – Synchronization of two clocks, PHC and node clock \(a.k.a system clock\) when using HW timestamping.
  * \(8\) Administrative access to the PHCs from deployment instances shall not be allowed, as that would interfere with the PHC management from the cloud platform software. The O-Cloud may provide direct read-only access to the PHC counters from the deployment instances.
  * \(9\) When the Slave \(subordinate\) PTP NIC is connected two at least two ports to the fronthaul network the PTP Slave \(subordinate\) NIC shall run the Alternative BMCA in order to select its best master clock.
